chapter_theme: Twelve songs at Madurai (மதுரை, also Koodal and the City of the Golden Lotus): courtesans and the wish for the feet, jnana that silences the sects, and praise that draws on Madurai's own stories, Siva's sports for Manikkavachakar and Sambandar's victory over the Jains.
structure_note: Courtesan and desire songs (959 to 963, 966); thanksgiving for jnana and the love that melts the bones (956); short pleas for jnana and compassion (964, 965); praise songs (957, 958); and 967, which recasts the book's opening song.

956.reading: The poet asks whether his bones will not melt in love as he names Murugan's shoulder that killed the demons, the vel that pierced the hill, the golden-anklet lotus feet, the kuthalam flower on his crown, the chest that took the forest girl and the six faces, and marvels at the jnana Murugan gave, in which the clamour of the sects, the arts, the five elements and the restless instruments of mind all fell silent. The praise tells how Ganapati, who loves chickpeas, candy, honey and millet dough, wrote the Bharata with one tusk on Meru when asked, and how Murugan circled the world on the peacock faster than the wind while Ganapati circled his father, and names him worshipped by the gods at Madurai.
956.nuance: The song is thanks rather than plea: தந்த ஞானம் இருந்தவாறு என், how wonderful the knowledge given. என்பெலாம் உருகு அன்பு, love that melts the bones, is a phrase of Saiva devotional poetry. The praise gives both sides of the fruit contest.

957.reading: The poet asks for grace to live and flourish in the state of reaching Murugan's paired feet. The praise calls him the younger brother of the elephant-faced one, the six-faced one, the guru who taught the Veda to Hara and to Brahma, the hero who cut down the demons, and the one who made his peacock dance to delight Uma and Chokkar of Madurai, whom none in heaven or earth, not Vishnu or Brahma, can know, and who calmed the gods' fear with the vel.
957.nuance: ஆதி அரனுக்கும் வேத முதல்வற்கும் ஆரணம் உரைத்த: here Murugan teaches both Siva and Brahma, not only binding Brahma for his ignorance.

958.reading: The poet seems to compare Murugan's coming to the sun's procession that lights the world and the moonlight that ends the dark, and asks that, singing the feet that grant honour, he may speak rich Tamil so that devotees rejoice, and be given boons. The praise names Murugan who delights when devotees bow saying 'Arahara, Sundara, Arumuga', son of Uma the creeper of the mountain, the beloved of the Kura girl, Saravana with kumkum on his chest, who grew up in golden Madurai.
958.nuance: The opening images (பரவு நெடுங்கதிர் உலகில் விரும்பிய பவனி, இருளை விடிந்தது நிலவாலே) have no clear subject and the reading of the first half is a guess. செந்தமிழ் உரைசெய அன்பரும் மகிழ: the gift sought is song that gladdens devotees.

959.reading: The poet describes courtesans who abuse some men and praise others, give one the betel from their mouths and another a helping hand, look only at money and embrace even a corpse in measure with it, give potions in the bedroom, embrace saying 'Karthigai is coming' and take a man's goods, say 'come once in Masi', call men while thinking of their property, finish with one and drive him off; he asks whether he must whirl like a yoked threshing bull in the hell called infatuation, and asks to be lifted from these pits, set among Murugan's devotees, ruled and given the goal. The praise names him the one who, like a guru learned in shastra and Veda, told the Saiva path into his father's ear, nephew of Rama who killed the demon who stole Janaki, husband of Indra's daughter, and the one who impaled the Jains, at Madurai.
959.nuance: பணத்தை நோக்குவர் பிணமது தழுவுவர்: they embrace even a corpse if the money is right, close to the Kural's image of the courtesan's embrace. The festival calls (கார்த்திகை வருது, மாத்தையில்) show the gifts expected at feasts. The remedy is company: உனடியவர் உடன் எனை அமர்த்தி. பல சமணரைக் கழுக்கள் ஏற்றிய identifies Murugan with Sambandar at Madurai.

960.reading: The poet describes a courtesan's display, fragrant hair, rolling spear-eyes, pearl smile, swinging chain, glittering body, the sari let fall to her feet, a walk like a peacock's dance, the net cast for men whom she makes beg and then gives disease and suffering, and asks when Murugan will seat in devotion to his garlanded feet one who leapt into their share, lost his mind and churns in the sea of sinful birth. The praise recounts Siva's Madurai sports: honouring Vathavurar as guru and revealing the jnana feet, turning jackals into horses for the king, dancing on the Vaigai bund and eating the woman's puttu, and calls Murugan the son of that madman; it also names the vel that ended the asuras and the green peacock like Rama.
960.nuance: நோய் பிணி கொடுத்து: the women give disease, a rare explicit charge. The praise is Madurai's own legend: வாதவூரனை, நரியின் குழுவை வாசியாம் என, வைகையாறின் மீது மண் எடுத்து, மாது தரு பிட்டு, Manikkavachakar's story. Several words in the last lines are corrupt.

961.reading: The poet describes women whose brows are bows, eyes arrows and breasts rutting elephants, whose coral lips and betel he thought pleasure to drink and eat, melting in their embrace with kumkum and sandal soaked in sweat, and asks whether even he, the rogue despised by all who took these women as his strength, will bow to Murugan's feet. The praise tells of Rama with Sita in the Dandaka forest killing Khara and Trisiras, Kumbhakarna and the ten-headed one with his bow, names Murugan the nephew of that Mukunda and the son of Uma, Gauri, Shankari, and the lotus-faced one born on the reed bed of the north, at Tamil Madurai.
961.nuance: பலருக்கும் கடை என்றனை இகழவும் ... வண்டனும் உனதடி பணிவேனோ: the self-abuse sets up the question whether even such a one can still bow. முழையுடல் சிதற and சங்கிலி மண்டப are obscure.

962.reading: The poet asks that, instead of dying on the breasts of oiled and garlanded women, wandering in delusion, roaming the world for wealth, hiding and becoming a thief and running in darkness, he chant and melt in clear jnana, study the Siva Purana books, and be given Murugan's feet. The praise names Siva, who from the letter A and the elements became the one form and the first, and danced in the hall before the gods while his consort sang, and calls Murugan his son, born as the maker of Tamil who, so that the Vedas, the six faiths, the three worlds, dharma, the tattvas and yoga might be kept, cured the Pandya Maran's hunchback and fever at Alavai.
962.nuance: திருடனாகி: the search for money to spend on women ends in theft. The praise says outright that Murugan was born as Sambandar (தமிழ்செய் மாறர் கூன் வெப்பொடு அன்று தவிர), who cured the king Koon Pandiyan of his hunch and fever.

963.reading: The poet asks whether he must wander every day, infatuated by women's songs and bangled hands, breasts like elephants on a golden hill, cuckoo speech, thread-thin waists, plantain thighs, moon faces and the trickery of spear-eyes. The praise names Murugan nephew of Vishnu who sleeps on the serpent in the sea, helped the elephant, became Vamana and wears the tulasi garland, the son born from the sparks of the eye of Siva clad in elephant hide with poison in his throat, at Koodal, the wonder-city of poets of the three Tamils.
963.nuance: கோவிற் பொறியால் வரு: Murugan born from the sparks of Siva's eye, stated plainly. The plea is a list of the woman's parts, each one a reason for wandering (உழல்வேனோ).

964.reading: A short song: the poet asks that, having bathed in the sea of the light of jnana found in the arts and crossed the sea of desire, he not stray in the many deluding disputes, and be given the life of knowledge of the Lord. The praise names Murugan who dwelt in the house of the Kura girl of the mountain, the hunter with the bow, bearer of the cock-banner, at Koodal.
964.nuance: பதிஞான வாழ்வு: the life sought is knowledge of Pati, the Lord. Two seas are set against each other, the sea of jnana to bathe in and the sea of desire to cross. திருவாணி கூடல் is unexplained.

965.reading: A very short song: the poet asks to be given the understanding of kindness to living beings, with truth and justice as its nature and discipline as its support. The praise calls Murugan the one of the sound of nada, the sea of jnana and the flawless nectar, at Koodal.
965.nuance: பூதத் தயவான போதம்: compassion to all creatures is asked for as a kind of understanding. The opening நீதத்துவம் can be split as நீதி தத்துவம் or otherwise, so the first line is uncertain.

966.reading: The poet lists courtesans as schemers, bed-quarrellers, goblins, women with mutilated noses, proud and fat, idle women who flatter, eat, dance and sing, who run down the street feigning modesty, coax and speak as if on a man's side, plunder and hook men for desire of wealth, and asks that their hold scatter and that Murugan place him on the one way that joins the nectar of grace and grant that he climb to his feet. The praise is a battle in drum syllables in which the vel destroyed the Suras, names Murugan who daily played with the millet-guarding daughter of the deer, and who whispered a meaning into the ear of Chokkan of south Koodal, the burner of the three cities with the woman as his half.
966.nuance: The plea is a list of feminine epithets ending in -கள் (காரிகள், மூளிகள், வீணிகள், பேசிகள்), a set form of the book. குனகிகள் பக்ஷம் போல பேசிகள், those who talk as if on your side, is the courtesan's double dealing. சொக்கன் காதில் ஓர் பொருள் places the teaching of Siva in Madurai.

967.reading: The poet asks Murugan, who gave grace to the word of the three-eyed Lord who chants him as the shakti, the hill and the seed of release, and whose feet the thirty-three classes of gods worship, to grant him the Sivam that dwells in devotees' hearts, the treasure held by the green-cloud Vishnu who loosed the arrow at the ten heads and drove the chariot to Arjuna's victory. The praise is a dance in drum syllables in which Murugan, equal to his dancing father, grants the nine siddhis, at the City of the Golden Lotus.
967.nuance: The song rebuilds the book's opening song 6 phrase by phrase: முத்து ... சத்தி ... முத்தி, the three-eyed one who chants, the thirty-three gods, the arrow at the ten heads, the chariot driven for a devotee, the green cloud. Here the treasure asked for is named as சிவம் in devotees' hearts. கனக பத்மபுரி is Madurai of the golden lotus tank. The phrase division of the first half is uncertain.

links.note: Both make the courtesan's embrace an embrace of a corpse, but in opposite directions: in the Kural the man who embraces her holds a stranger's corpse in a dark room; in 959 the women, looking only at money, will embrace even a corpse.
1 says only that Ganapati first wrote on the first mountain; 956 tells the story fully, that he wrote the Bharata with one tusk on Meru when he was asked.

967 recasts the book's opening song almost formula by formula, the three-eyed Lord's chant of the seed of release, the thirty-three gods, the arrow at the ten heads and the chariot driven by the green-cloud Vishnu, and names the treasure sought as Sivam in devotees' hearts.
Both fault the courtesan's double dealing: the Naladiyar's eel shows one end to the snake and the other to the fish, and 966's women talk as if on a man's side while hooking him for his wealth.

956 asks whether love will not melt all his bones (நெக்கு என்பெலாம் உருகு அன்பு) as he names Murugan's feet, crown and faces. Tirumular says that even making one's bones the firewood (என்பே விறகா) and frying one's flesh reaches nothing, and only those who melt with love (அன்போடு உருகி அகங்குழைவார்) reach the gem. The song takes up the Tirumanthiram's measure, bones and melting love, and turns the ascetic's burnt bones into bones that melt in devotion.

956 marvels at the jnana Murugan gave, in which the clamour of the quarrelling sects (சிலுகிடு சமயப் பங்கவாதிகள் கதறிய வெகுசொல்) fell silent along with the arts and the senses. Tirumular says those who saw the six sects did not see him (ஆறு சமயமும் கண்டவர் கண்டிலர்) and urges clarity and settling. Both put the knowledge of God past the sects' disputes; the song reports it as a gift received.

959 says the courtesans call men while weighing their property (அழைப்பர் ஆஸ்திகள் கருதுவர்), look only at money and drive a man off when he is finished. Kural 912 tells one to weigh and avoid women who weigh the profit and then speak of their virtue (பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும்). The song shows the weighing in action, the festival calls and the potions; the Kural gives the rule that the man should weigh them in return.

962 traces the chase after women into roaming for money, hiding and becoming a thief, then a man of darkness (திருடனாகி ... திமிரனாகி), and asks instead for clear jnana (தெளியும் ஞானம்). Kural 287 calls stealth a dark knowledge (களவென்னும் காரறிவாண்மை) absent in those who love measure. The song places theft on the same scale of dark and clear knowing and shows desire as the road to it.

964 asks that, having crossed the sea of desire (ஆசைக் கடலேறி) and bathed in the sea of jnana, he be given the life of knowledge of the Lord (பதிஞான வாழ்வு). Kural 370 says that giving up craving, never filled by nature (ஆரா இயற்கை அவா), at once gives an unchanging nature (பேரா இயற்கை). The Kural states the exchange; the song names what the unchanging state is, a life in knowledge of Pati.

965 asks for kindness to living beings as a kind of understanding (பூதத் தயவான போதம்), with truth and discipline as its ground. Kural 249 says that virtue done without kindness is like a man without clarity seeing the truth (தெருளாதான் மெய்ப்பொருள் கண்டற்றால்). Both tie compassion to knowing: the Kural makes the lack of one like the lack of the other, and the song asks for them as one gift.

966 lists the courtesans who coax and speak as if on a man's side (குனகிகள் பக்ஷம் போல பேசிகள்) and hook men by desire of wealth (பொருளாசைக் கொளுவிகள்). Kural 911 says the sweet words of women who desire wealth and not love (அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும்) bring harm. The song's 'as if on your side' is the Kural's sweet word without love, named from the man's experience of it.

Song 960: corrupt glyphs in ரா¡£ணமயி (line 23); the line வேத மீண கமலக் கணர் மெய் பச்சை ரகுராம ... is hard to recover.
